{{Short description|Describes state evolution of a linear system}}
{{Technical|date=December 2018}}

In [[control theory]] and [[dynamical systems theory]], the '''state-transition matrix''' is a [[matrix function]] that describes how the [[State space representation|state]] of a [[linear system]] changes over time. Essentially, if the system's state is known at an initial time {{tmath|t_0}}, the state-transition matrix allows for the calculation of the state at any future time {{tmath|t}}.

The matrix is used to find the general solution to the homogeneous [[linear differential equation]] <math>\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{A}(t) \mathbf{x}(t)</math> and is also a key component in finding the full solution for the non-homogeneous (input-driven) case.

For [[Linear time-invariant system|linear time-invariant (LTI) systems]], where the matrix <math>\mathbf{A}</math> is constant, the state-transition matrix is the [[matrix exponential]] {{tmath|\textstyle \exp{(\mathbf{A}(t-t_0))} }}. In the more complex [[Time-variant system|time-variant]] case, where <math>\mathbf{A}(t)</math> can change over time, there is no simple formula, and the matrix is typically found by calculating the [[Peano–Baker series]].

==Linear systems solutions==
The state-transition matrix is used to find the solution to a general [[state-space representation]] of a [[linear system]] in the following form
<math display="block">\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{A}(t) \mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf{B}(t) \mathbf{u}(t), \;\mathbf{x}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_0, </math>
where <math>\mathbf{x}(t)</math> are the states of the system; <math>\mathbf{u}(t)</math> is the input signal; <math>\mathbf{A}(t)</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}(t)</math> are [[matrix function]]s; and <math>\mathbf{x}_0</math> is the initial condition at {{tmath|t_0}}. Using the state-transition matrix {{tmath|\mathbf{\Phi}(t, \tau) }}, the solution is given by:<ref name=baaschl>{{cite journal |last1= Baake |first1= Michael |last2= Schlaegel |first2= Ulrike |date=2011 |title= The Peano Baker Series |journal= Proceedings of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics |volume= 275 |pages= 155–159 |doi= 10.1134/S0081543811080098 |s2cid= 119133539}}</ref><ref name=rugh>{{cite book |last1= Rugh |first1= Wilson |date= 1996 |title= Linear System Theory |publisher= Prentice Hall |location= Upper Saddle River, New Jersey |isbn= 0-13-441205-2}}</ref>
<math display="block">\mathbf{x}(t)= \mathbf{\Phi} (t, t_0)\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t \mathbf{\Phi}(t, \tau)\mathbf{B}(\tau)\mathbf{u}(\tau)\ d\tau.</math>

The first term is known as the '''zero-input response''' and represents how the system's state would evolve in the absence of any input. The second term is known as the '''zero-state response''' and defines how the inputs impact the system.

==Peano–Baker series==
The most general transition matrix is given by a [[product integral]], referred to as the '''Peano–Baker series''':
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathbf{\Phi}(t,\tau) = \mathbf{I} &+ \int_\tau^t\mathbf{A}(\sigma_1)\,d\sigma_1 \\
&+ \int_\tau^t\mathbf{A}(\sigma_1)\int_\tau^{\sigma_1}\mathbf{A}(\sigma_2)\,d\sigma_2\,d\sigma_1 \\
&+ \int_\tau^t\mathbf{A}(\sigma_1)\int_\tau^{\sigma_1}\mathbf{A}(\sigma_2)\int_\tau^{\sigma_2}\mathbf{A}(\sigma_3)\,d\sigma_3\,d\sigma_2\,d\sigma_1 \\
&+ \cdots,
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\mathbf{I}</math> is the  [[identity matrix]]. This matrix converges uniformly and absolutely to a solution that exists and is unique.<ref name=rugh /> The series has a formal sum that can be written as
<math display="block">\mathbf{\Phi}(t,\tau) = \exp \mathcal{T}\int_\tau^t\mathbf{A}(\sigma)\,d\sigma, </math>
where <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is the [[time-ordering]] operator, used to ensure that the repeated [[product integral]] is in proper order. The [[Magnus expansion]] provides a means for evaluating this product.

==Other properties==
The state transition matrix <math> \mathbf{\Phi}</math> satisfies the following relationships. These relationships are generic to the [[product integral]].

# It is continuous and has continuous derivatives.
# It is never singular; in fact <math display="inline">\mathbf{\Phi}^{-1}(t, \tau) = \mathbf{ \Phi}(\tau, t)</math> and {{tmath|1= \textstyle \mathbf{\Phi}^{-1}(t, \tau)\mathbf{\Phi}(t, \tau) = \mathbf I}}, where <math>\mathbf I</math> is the identity matrix.
# <math>\mathbf{\Phi}(t, t) = \mathbf I</math> for all {{tmath|t}}.<ref>{{cite book |first= Roger W. |last= Brockett |date= 1970 |title= Finite Dimensional Linear Systems |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn= 978-0-471-10585-5}}</ref>
# <math>\mathbf{\Phi}(t_2, t_1)\mathbf{\Phi}(t_1, t_0) = \mathbf{\Phi}(t_2, t_0)</math> for all {{tmath| t_0 \leq  t_1 \leq t_2 }}.
# It satisfies the differential equation <math display="inline">\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0)= \mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0)</math> with initial conditions {{tmath|=1 \mathbf{\Phi}(t_0, t_0) = \mathbf I }}.
# The state-transition matrix {{tmath| \mathbf{\Phi}(t,\tau) }}, given by <math display="inline">\mathbf{\Phi}(t, \tau)\equiv\mathbf{U}(t)\mathbf{U}^{-1}(\tau)</math> where the <math>n \times n</math> matrix <math>\mathbf{U}(t)</math> is the [[Fundamental matrix (linear differential equation)|fundamental solution matrix]] that satisfies <math>\dot{\mathbf{U}}(t)=\mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{U}(t)</math> with initial condition {{tmath|1= \mathbf{U}(t_0) = \mathbf I }}.
# Given the state <math>\mathbf{x}(\tau)</math> at any time {{tmath|\tau}}, the state at any other time <math>t</math> is given by the mapping {{tmath|1= \mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{\Phi}(t,\tau)\mathbf{x}(\tau) }}.

==Estimation of the state-transition matrix==

In the [[time-invariant]] case, we can define {{tmath| \mathbf{\Phi} }}, using the [[matrix exponential]], as {{tmath|1= \textstyle \mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0) = \exp{(\mathbf{A}(t - t_0))} }}. <ref>{{cite journal |last1= Reyneke |first1= Pieter V. |date= 2012 |title= Polynomial Filtering: To any degree on irregularly sampled data |journal= Automatika |volume= 53 |issue= 4 |pages= 382–397 |doi= 10.7305/automatika.53-4.248 |s2cid= 40282943 |url= https://hrcak.srce.hr/clanak/138435 |doi-access= free |hdl= 2263/21017 |hdl-access= free }}</ref>

In the [[time-variant]] case, the state-transition matrix <math>\mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0)</math> can be estimated from the solutions of the differential equation <math>\dot{\mathbf{u}}(t)=\mathbf{A}(t)\mathbf{u}(t)</math> with initial conditions <math>\mathbf{u}(t_0)</math> given by {{tmath| \textstyle [1,\ 0,\ \ldots,\ 0]^\mathrm{T} }}, {{tmath| \textstyle [0,\ 1,\ \ldots,\ 0]^\mathrm{T} }},&nbsp;..., {{tmath| \textstyle [0,\ 0,\ \ldots,\ 1]^\mathrm{T} }}. The corresponding solutions provide the <math>n</math> columns of matrix {{tmath| \mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0) }}. Now, from property 4, <math display="inline">\mathbf{\Phi}(t, \tau) = \mathbf{\Phi}(t, t_0)\mathbf{\Phi}(\tau, t_0)^{-1}</math> for all {{tmath| t_0 \leq  \tau \leq t }}. The state-transition matrix must be determined before analysis on the time-varying solution can continue.
